title: Get safe drinking water
intro: Readings for when tap water is off or may be unsafe: how to treat water, where to find water already in your home, and how to store it. It also points to warnings about water that boiling or bleach cannot fix, such as salt water and flood water.

choices.label: Tap water is off or might be unsafe
choices.hint: Boil-water notice, earthquake, flood, broken main

read.label: Ways to treat water of uncertain quality
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004). When to treat water, why to let particles settle or strain first, and boiling instructions. Says boiling and bleach do not remove chemicals.

read.label: Keep water safe during and after a flood
read.note: FDA fact sheet (2007): use unexposed bottled water, how to boil or bleach cloudy water, and what to do if your well was flooded.

read.label: After an earthquake: check for water leaks and shut the main valve
read.note: FEMA P-530 Earthquake Safety at Home (2020) checklist page: where to look for leaking pipes and where the home's main water valve usually is.

choices.label: I can boil water
choices.hint: Stove, camp stove, grill or fire is available

read.label: How long to boil water, and how to fix the taste
read.note: Hesperian, New Where There Is No Doctor (2017): rolling boil time, longer time in high mountains, and shaking cooled water to improve taste. Also covers bleach on the same page.

read.label: Boiling: the FEMA/Red Cross method
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004) calls boiling the safest method and describes boil time, cooling, and pouring between containers for taste.

read.label: WHO: boiling, chlorine, and their limits
read.note: WHO emergency technical note (2013) on boiling and chemical disinfection; notes some parasites such as cryptosporidium resist chlorine.

read.label: Bleach drops per gallon and the smell test
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004). Gives a dose for bleach of 5.25–6% strength (stated on page 13), the waiting time, and what to do if no chlorine smell remains.

read.label: Bleach chart for 1 liter up to a 200-liter barrel
read.note: Hesperian (2017) chart for 5% bleach. Says to read the label for the percent of chlorine, use more if weaker, and avoid bleach with soap or perfume.

read.label: CERT manual: bleach amounts for clear and cloudy water
read.note: FEMA CERT Participant Manual (2019): boiling, tablets, or non-perfumed bleach, with drop counts for clear versus cloudy water and a re-dose step.

read.label: How much chlorine to use, and what 'free chlorine' means
read.note: Hesperian Community Guide to Environmental Health (2012). Explains why water should smell slightly of chlorine, and doubling the dose for cloudy water. Sources differ on drop counts; each states its bleach strength.

choices.label: I have a filter, tablets, or only sunlight
choices.hint: Camping filter, purification tablets, clear bottles

read.label: Filter, then disinfect: collecting and purifying natural water
read.note: National Park Service page. Says filtration by itself does not purify water and must be followed by boiling or chemical treatment.

read.label: Picture guide: treating water with chlorine tablets
read.note: WHO technical note (2013) diagram for clear versus dirty water with tablets; says tablet number depends on container size and tablet strength, so check the maker's instructions.

read.label: Sunlight disinfection with clear bottles
read.note: Hesperian (2017): how to use clear plastic bottles in full sun, how long to leave them, and why it works best near the equator.

read.label: Video: how backcountry water filters work (REI, 4 min)
read.note: Explains which germs filters remove and why viruses may need boiling or chemical treatment as well.

choices.label: Find water already inside the house
choices.hint: Water heater or geyser, pipes, ice

read.label: Hidden water sources in your home
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004): using water in the hot-water tank, pipes and ice; which sources not to drink (toilet tank, radiators, waterbeds, pools); shutting the main valve.

read.label: Table of safe and unsafe water sources at home
read.note: Older FEMA Are You Ready? guide. Safe/unsafe table, notes that pool and spa water can be used for hygiene only, and how to drain pipes and the water heater.

read.label: Your water heater as an emergency water source
read.note: FEMA P-530 (2020): typical water heater capacity, usable if it was strapped and is not damaged; suggests storing purification tablets.

read.label: After an earthquake: check the water heater first
read.note: FEMA P-530 (2020) checklist: signs of damage, shutting off gas, water and power, and saving drained water if it is clean.

choices.label: I live in an apartment or high-rise
choices.hint: Taps slow or stop when the power is out

read.label: Why a power cut can also stop water and sewage
read.note: Norwegian civil protection guide (2024): a power failure can mean home water supply and sewage systems stop working normally; it suggests being ready to manage for one week.

read.label: What happens to tap water when water utilities lose power
read.note: EPA Power Resilience Guide (2023), written for water utilities: pumps can stop producing water, pressure loss can let contaminants into pipes, and sewage can back up into homes.

read.label: Water already inside your home: water heater, pipes, ice
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross (2004) lists hot-water tanks as emergency drinking-water sources. Norway's guidance below recommends hygiene use only; the sources disagree.

read.label: Norway's differing advice on water-heater water
read.note: Norwegian civil protection guide (2024): water from the heater may be used in a crisis, but should not be used for drinking.

choices.label: Get water from rain, a stream, pool or well
choices.hint: No stored water left, borewell or tubewell

read.label: Emergency outdoor water sources
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004) lists rain, streams, ponds and springs, which to avoid, that seawater needs distilling, and not to drink flood water.

read.label: Make collected rainwater safe to drink
read.note: Hesperian (2012): cleaning roofs and tanks, letting first rains run through, covering and screening, and adding chlorine or a filter.

read.label: If your well has been flooded
read.note: FDA fact sheet (2007): a flooded well should be tested and disinfected; contact the local or state health department.

read.label: Using roof, river or water-heater water for washing
read.note: Norwegian civil protection guide: such water may be badly contaminated and unsuitable after chemical releases or fallout; check with authorities first.

choices.label: Only river, harbor or flood water nearby
choices.hint: City river, canal, bay or flooded streets

read.label: Which outdoor water to avoid, and salt water
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004) lists outdoor sources to treat first, water to avoid (floating material, odor, dark color), salt water only if distilled, and no flood water.

read.label: Boiling and bleach do not remove salt or most chemicals
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004): boiling or chlorination kills most germs but leaves heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals. Page 14 describes distilling.

read.label: What flood water can carry
read.note: CERT Hazard Annexes (2019), hurricane section: floodwaters may hold oil, gasoline, chemicals, bacteria and raw sewage, plus hidden downed power lines.

choices.label: Water may contain fuel, chemicals or sewage
choices.hint: Odd smell or color, spill, flood water, industrial area

read.label: Why filtering and disinfecting will not remove toxic chemicals
read.note: Hesperian (2012): settle or filter, then disinfect, for germs only. States water with toxic chemicals is never safe for drinking, bathing or washing clothes.

read.label: Toxic pollution in water: what it is and how it is found
read.note: Hesperian (2012): chemicals from industry, mining and nature are usually invisible; lab testing is how they are detected.

read.label: Distillation: the one home method listed for salts and chemicals
read.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004) describes distilling with a pot, lid and hanging cup and says it removes heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals.

choices.label: Keep treated water clean once you have it
choices.hint: Containers, dippers, how much per person

read.label: Stop stored water from getting dirty again
read.note: Hesperian (2017): pouring or using a clean dipper, cleaning containers, covers, and the usual daily amount for drinking and cooking.

read.label: WHO: storing treated water and handwashing
read.note: WHO technical note (2013): covered, cool, dark storage, wide-neck containers with lids, and fitting a tap to avoid hands touching water.

read.label: How much water people need in emergencies
read.note: WHO technical note on minimum water quantities for survival and how needs vary with climate and health (based on Sphere standards).

limits.text: Boiling or chlorination kills most germs but does not remove heavy metals, salts, or most other chemicals.
Water that contains toxic chemicals is never safe for drinking, bathing, or washing clothes; home treatment methods do not make it safe.
Do not drink flood water, or water from toilet tanks, radiators, waterbeds, or pools and spas.
If the gas was turned off to drain the water heater, a professional is needed to turn it back on.
If bleach-treated water still has no slight bleach smell after a second dose, throw it out and find another source.
A flooded well should be tested and disinfected; contact your local or state health department for advice.
Some parasites, notably cryptosporidium, are resistant to chlorine.
Collected rain or river water may be unsuitable after chemical releases or nuclear fallout; seek information from authorities first.
When water utilities lose power, pressure loss can let contaminants into the drinking water pipes.
Do not use salt water unless you distill it first.
Floodwaters may carry oil, gasoline, chemicals, bacteria and raw sewage, and can hide downed power lines.

prepare.note: FEMA Are You Ready? guide (2020): water per person per day, and suggested numbers of days to keep on hand.

prepare.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004): daily needs, extra for heat, children, nursing mothers and sick people, and a two-week storage goal.

prepare.label: Choosing and preparing containers for stored water
prepare.note: FEMA/Red Cross booklet (2004): bottled versus home-filled water, which containers to avoid; page 11 covers cleaning, filling, labeling and replacing.

prepare.label: CERT tips: which plastic bottles to use and when to replace
prepare.note: FEMA CERT manual (2019): look for recycling symbol 1, avoid milk jugs and glass, store cool and dark, replace every six months.

prepare.label: Strap your water heater before an earthquake
prepare.note: FEMA P-530 (2020): why unstrapped heaters fail, fire and carbon monoxide risks, and that a strapped heater is an emergency water source.

prepare.label: Collecting rainwater from a roof
prepare.note: Hesperian (2012): which roofs are safe to collect from, keeping barrels clean, and tanks above or below ground.

prepare.label: Add a water purification system to your kit
prepare.note: FEMA Are You Ready? (2020) list of extra kit items, including a water purification system and hand sanitizer.
